title: Node.js Basics
content: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine. It lets developers run JavaScript on the server and uses an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model that makes it well suited for network applications.

title: Express.js Routing
content: Express.js is a minimal web framework for Node.js. Routing defines how an application responds to client requests for a specific endpoint and HTTP method such as GET, POST, PUT, or DELETE.

title: Middleware in Express
content: Middleware functions in Express have access to the request and response objects and the next function. They are used for logging, authentication, parsing request bodies, and handling errors.

title: Introduction to PostgreSQL
content: PostgreSQL is a powerful open-source relational database that supports SQL, transactions, indexes, and JSON data. It is known for reliability, extensibility, and standards compliance.

title: SQL Joins Explained
content: A SQL join combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column. Common types include inner join, left join, right join, and full outer join.

title: Database Indexing
content: An index is a data structure that speeds up data retrieval in a database at the cost of extra storage and slower writes. B-tree indexes are the default in most relational databases.

title: MongoDB Overview
content: MongoDB is a NoSQL document database that stores data as flexible JSON-like documents. It scales horizontally and works well when the schema evolves frequently.

title: SQL vs NoSQL
content: Relational databases enforce a fixed schema and support complex joins, while NoSQL databases offer flexible schemas and horizontal scaling. The right choice depends on data shape and access patterns.

title: JavaScript Closures
content: A closure is a function that remembers the variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished executing. Closures power callbacks, module patterns, and data privacy.

title: Promises and Async/Await
content: Promises represent the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. Async/await is syntax built on promises that makes asynchronous code read like synchronous code.

title: The JavaScript Event Loop
content: The event loop lets JavaScript perform non-blocking operations despite being single-threaded. It processes the call stack, then the microtask queue, then the callback queue.

title: REST API Design
content: REST is an architectural style for designing networked applications using stateless HTTP requests. Good REST APIs use clear resource names, proper status codes, and consistent versioning.

title: HTTP Status Codes
content: HTTP status codes tell the client how a request went. 200 means success, 404 means not found, 401 means unauthorized, and 500 means an internal server error.

title: JSON Web Tokens
content: A JSON Web Token is a compact, signed token used for authentication. The server issues it after login and the client sends it with later requests to prove identity.

title: Password Hashing with bcrypt
content: Passwords should never be stored in plain text. bcrypt is a slow hashing algorithm with a built-in salt that makes brute-force and rainbow table attacks much harder.

title: Introduction to Git
content: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes in source code. Developers use commits, branches, and merges to collaborate without overwriting each other's work.

title: Git Branching Strategies
content: Branching strategies like Git Flow and trunk-based development define how teams create, review, and merge branches. Short-lived branches reduce merge conflicts.

title: Docker Fundamentals
content: Docker packages an application and its dependencies into a container that runs the same way everywhere. Images are built from Dockerfiles and containers are running instances of images.

title: Docker Compose
content: Docker Compose lets you define and run multi-container applications using a YAML file. It is commonly used to start an app, a database, and a cache together for local development.

title: Introduction to Kubernetes
content: Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform that automates deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications across clusters of machines.

title: Big O Notation
content: Big O notation describes how the running time or memory usage of an algorithm grows as the input size increases. Common classes include O(1), O(log n), O(n), and O(n^2).

title: Binary Search
content: Binary search finds a target in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search range. It runs in O(log n) time, which is far faster than linear search for large inputs.

title: Hash Tables
content: A hash table maps keys to values using a hash function to compute an index. Average lookup, insert, and delete operations take constant time, though collisions must be handled.

title: Linked Lists
content: A linked list is a linear data structure where each node points to the next. Insertion and deletion are fast, but random access is slow compared to arrays.

title: Trees and Binary Search Trees
content: A binary search tree keeps smaller values in the left subtree and larger values in the right. Balanced trees give logarithmic search, insertion, and deletion.

title: Graph Traversal: BFS and DFS
content: Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level using a queue, while depth-first search goes as deep as possible using a stack or recursion. Both run in O(V + E) time.

title: Dynamic Programming
content: Dynamic programming solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing results to avoid recomputation. Classic examples are Fibonacci, knapsack, and longest common subsequence.

title: Sorting Algorithms
content: Sorting algorithms like merge sort and quicksort run in O(n log n) on average. Simple algorithms like bubble sort and insertion sort run in O(n^2) and are mostly educational.

title: Recursion
content: Recursion is a technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller versions of a problem. Every recursive function needs a base case to stop and avoid stack overflow.

title: Introduction to Search Engines
content: A search engine crawls documents, builds an index, and ranks results for a user query. The core data structure is the inverted index, which maps each term to the documents containing it.

title: Inverted Index
content: An inverted index stores, for every unique term, a list of documents where it appears along with positions or frequencies. It allows fast full-text search without scanning every document.

title: Tokenization and Stop Words
content: Tokenization splits text into individual terms, usually words. Stop words such as the, is, and of are often removed because they carry little meaning for search ranking.

title: Stemming and Lemmatization
content: Stemming chops word endings to reduce words like running and runs to a common root. Lemmatization uses vocabulary and grammar to return the proper base form of a word.

title: TF-IDF Ranking
content: TF-IDF scores a term by how often it appears in a document and how rare it is across all documents. Terms that are frequent in one document but rare overall get higher weights.

title: BM25 Ranking Function
content: BM25 is a ranking function that improves on TF-IDF by saturating term frequency and normalizing for document length. It is the default scoring method in many search engines.

title: Web Crawling Basics
content: A web crawler downloads pages, extracts links, and follows them to discover new pages. Good crawlers respect robots.txt, limit request rates, and avoid fetching duplicate content.

title: Elasticsearch Overview
content: Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene. It exposes a REST API and supports full-text search, filtering, and aggregations over JSON documents.

title: PostgreSQL Full-Text Search
content: PostgreSQL offers built-in full-text search using tsvector and tsquery types with GIN indexes. It supports stemming, ranking, and phrase search without any external service.

title: Precision and Recall
content: Precision is the fraction of retrieved results that are relevant, while recall is the fraction of relevant documents that were retrieved. Search evaluation often balances the two.

title: Caching with Redis
content: Redis is an in-memory key-value store used for caching, sessions, and queues. Caching frequent query results in Redis can dramatically reduce database load and response time.

title: HTML and CSS Fundamentals
content: HTML defines the structure of a web page while CSS controls its appearance. Together with JavaScript they form the foundation of front-end web development.

title: CSS Flexbox and Grid
content: Flexbox arranges items in one dimension, either a row or a column, while CSS Grid handles two-dimensional layouts. Both make responsive page layouts much easier.

title: React Components and Props
content: React builds user interfaces from reusable components. Props pass data from parent to child components, and state lets a component remember and update its own data.

title: React Hooks
content: Hooks like useState and useEffect let function components manage state and side effects. Custom hooks allow sharing stateful logic between components.

title: TypeScript Introduction
content: TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript and compiles to plain JavaScript. Type checking catches many bugs at compile time and improves editor autocompletion.

title: Unit Testing with Jest
content: Jest is a JavaScript testing framework with built-in assertions, mocking, and coverage reports. Unit tests verify that small pieces of code behave correctly in isolation.

title: CI/CD Pipelines
content: Continuous integration automatically builds and tests code on every commit, while continuous delivery automates deployment. Tools like GitHub Actions run these pipelines.

title: Web Security Basics
content: Common web vulnerabilities include SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and cross-site request forgery. Validating input, escaping output, and using parameterized queries prevent most attacks.

title: Microservices Architecture
content: Microservices split an application into small, independently deployable services that communicate over APIs. They improve scalability and team autonomy but add operational complexity.

title: System Design: Scaling a Web App
content: Scaling a web application involves load balancing, caching, database replication, and sharding. Horizontal scaling adds more machines, while vertical scaling adds more power to one machine.
